Do We Need an LLM to Know Why Sources Conflict?
Decision Models for Knowledge-Conflict Typing in RAG

Parv Khatri Affiliation: Independent Researcher Email: khatriparv@gmail.com    Harshul Jain Affiliation: Independent Researcher Email: harshuljain1393@gmail.com    Mehak Kapoor Affiliation: Independent Researcher Email: mehakkapoor9873@gmail.com    Tanya Sah Affiliation: Independent Researcher Email: tanyasah20@gmail.com
Abstract

When the sources retrieved for a query disagree, the right response depends on why they disagree: a question with several valid answers, a contested topic, stale information and a false source each call for different behaviour. Cattan et al. (2025) showed that telling a generator the conflict type improves its responses by about 24 points, but that predicting the type is hard even for frontier LLMs. We study whether typed decision models, which return probabilities over fixed options in a single forward pass instead of generating text, can do this classification fast and cheaply. Using the Conflicts benchmark and the original paper’s prompt verbatim, we evaluate all 11 decision models served by one commercial inference gateway, from 7 providers, against Gemini models on identical inputs. Asked directly, the decision models reach 50.0–67.0 % accuracy; 10 of the 11 match or exceed Gemini 2.5 Flash, the paper’s model (61.3 %), at 4–39 ×\times lower billed cost (2 were free) and 2.6–6.0 ×\times lower latency. The current Gemini 3.8 Flash (70.0 %) is significantly more accurate than 8 of them, but sending each decision model’s least confident quarter of queries to it gives a cascade statistically tied with it for 8 of the 11, at 25–37 % of its cost. End to end, answers generated with the types of 10 of the 11 follow the expected behaviour as often as with the LLM’s types. Decomposing the taxonomy into yes/no questions lowers accuracy for every model, and a repair fitted on one model does not transfer. Pre-specified diagnostics show that dates play no measurable role and that sensitivity to source order varies widely between models. Decision models detect a planted false source less reliably than the LLM as hard labels, but their probabilities still separate planted from clean sources. We release code, prompts and all model outputs at https://github.com/Parv17k/decision-models-conflict-typing.

1 Introduction

Search-augmented language models answer from retrieved web pages, and those pages often disagree. The disagreement can have very different causes. A question may be underspecified and admit several correct answers; it may touch a contested topic on which reasonable sources differ; the answer may have changed over time, so some pages are stale; or a page may simply be wrong. Each case calls for a different response: combine the answers, present the viewpoints neutrally, prefer the most recent information, or ignore the unreliable source. Cattan et al. (2025) formalised this as a five-way taxonomy, released Conflicts, a benchmark of 458 search queries annotated by experts with their conflict type, and showed that giving a generator the gold type raises the share of responses with the expected behaviour by about 24 points. Predicting the type is harder: the best LLM they tested, Gemini 2.5 Flash, reached 65.3% accuracy.

Conflict typing is a classification problem. It is made once per query, before the answer is written, and its output is one of five labels. A classifier for it should therefore be fast enough to sit in front of every search-augmented request, cheap enough to run on all of them, and calibrated enough that its uncertainty can be acted on. A recent class of models, typed decision models, is designed for this setting: they take unstructured context and typed questions and return probabilities over the allowed answers in a single forward pass, without generating text (TypeSafe AI, 2026a). Since the first such model, several providers have released their own, and one inference gateway now serves 11 of them behind a common interface. Existing evaluations cover classification, NLI and judging benchmarks, mostly for a single model (Deußer et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b; Duan et al., 2026), but none covers deciding why retrieved sources conflict, a task that requires reading many documents at once and reasoning about their mutual relation rather than about one text.

Can decision models, as a class, serve as this decision layer? And if only some can, what sets them apart? Our study (Figure 1) makes five contributions.

(1) A census of decision models on conflict typing.

We evaluate every decision model served by one commercial gateway (11 models from 7 providers) on Conflicts under the original paper’s protocol: the same input representation, the same category definitions and examples taken verbatim from the paper’s source, and Gemini rerun on identical inputs so that every comparison is paired (§6.1). 10 of the 11 models match or exceed the paper’s LLM at a fraction of its cost and latency; the current Gemini 3.8 Flash is significantly more accurate than 8 of them.

(2) A formulation study.

Decomposing the taxonomy into yes/no questions lowers accuracy for all 11 models, and a repair fitted on one model helps none, leaving the direct question as the reliable format (§6.2).

(3) Cost-quality cascades.

Decision models’ confidence ranks their own errors, so sending their least certain queries to an LLM is effective: with a quarter of the queries escalated to Gemini 3.8 Flash, 8 of the 11 cascades are statistically tied with the LLM alone at 25–37 % of its cost (§6.3).

(4) Pre-specified diagnostics.

We test whether decision models depend on publication dates, are sensitive to source order, or miss a single false source among agreeing ones (§6.4). Dates play no measurable role, order sensitivity varies from model to model, and a planted false source shows in the probabilities more than in the top answer.

(5) An end-to-end test.

Given to a generator, the types of 10 of the 11 decision models yield answers that follow the expected behaviour as often as with the LLM’s types, under both judges we specified (§6.5).

Every setting and every later addition was fixed in writing before it was run (§5). We release the code, prompts, splits and all model outputs at https://github.com/Parv17k/decision-models-conflict-typing.

2 Related Work

Knowledge conflicts in retrieval-augmented generation.

Xu et al. (2024) survey conflicts between a model’s parametric knowledge and its context, among retrieved contexts, and within the model’s memory. Work on inter-context conflicts has largely studied one cause at a time, such as substituted entities (Longpre et al., 2021), contradictions in Wikipedia (Hou et al., 2024), contested questions (Wan et al., 2024), temporal or geographic context (Zhang and Choi, 2021), freshness (Vu et al., 2024) or conflicting contexts in open-domain QA (Liu et al., 2024). Cattan et al. (2025) unify these causes into a taxonomy with expected behaviours and release Conflicts, the first benchmark annotated with the conflict type; we build directly on it. Methods for resolving conflicts include multi-agent debate over documents (Wang et al., 2025), reasoning traces learned by fine-tuning (Mishra et al., 2025), and a two-stage detector that sends an embedding classifier’s uncertain cases to an LLM (Wang et al., 2026). None of these uses a typed decision model.

Typed decision models.

A typed decision model answers typed questions (choice, score, yes/no) over a supplied state with probabilities over the allowed answers, trained for calibration rather than generation. The class was introduced with Jev (TypeSafe AI, 2026a), and hosted and open-weight alternatives followed; open reimplementations have been benchmarked against the hosted reference (Weng et al., 2026). Independent evaluations, so far mostly of the first model, find decision models competitive with frontier LLMs on knowledge, classification and NLI benchmarks at a fraction of the cost (Deußer et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b), calibrated on choice questions but biased towards yes when many yes/no questions share a request (Deußer et al., 2026; Li and Wagle, 2026), not always coherent across logically related questions (Li et al., 2026a), weaker as inputs grow long (Duan et al., 2026), and vulnerable to natural-looking context that flips their decisions (Xu et al., 2026). As judges, they are cheaper than LLMs but share their most confident errors (Rao and Callison-Burch, 2026), and a confidence-gated cascade to an LLM can match the LLM at lower cost (Li et al., 2026c). Closest to our setting, Huang et al. (2026) use a decision model to decide whether one report supports or contradicts another. Duan et al. (2026) compare several decision models on general benchmarks; no prior work compares them on typing the conflict among many retrieved sources.

Cascades and selective prediction.

Routing easy inputs to a cheap model and hard ones to an expensive model is an established way to trade cost for quality (Chen et al., 2023); its effectiveness depends on how well the cheap model’s confidence ranks its own errors, the quantity studied in selective classification (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017). We measure this directly for every decision model on conflict typing and compare against random escalation.

3 Task and Data

Taxonomy.

We use the taxonomy of Cattan et al. (2025). Given a query and its retrieved sources, the conflict is one of: No conflict (the sources agree, up to wording or granularity); Complementary information (the answers differ but can all be correct, e.g. because the query is underspecified); Conflicting opinions or research outcomes (a subjective or contested topic with genuinely opposing views); Outdated information (a factual question on which sources disagree because the answer changed over time); and Misinformation (a factual question on which some sources are wrong).

Data.

Conflicts contains 458 queries drawn from ConflictingQA (Wan et al., 2024), the geographic and temporal subsets of SituatedQA (Zhang and Choi, 2021), FreshQA (Vu et al., 2024) and QACC (Liu et al., 2024), each with the top Google Search results (9.2 on average), the conflict type assigned by expert annotators, and, for the types with a single correct answer, that answer. Each result carries a URL, title, snippet, publication date when available, and the 512-token segment of the page most relevant to the query. The released file has no split. We draw a stratified development split of 52 queries with a fixed seed and use it only to choose settings; the remaining 406 queries form the test split on which we report (Table 1). Misinformation has only five instances in the whole dataset, a limitation we return to in §6.4 by constructing a planted variant.

Metric.

Following Cattan et al. (2025), the primary metric is five-class accuracy. We also report macro-F1 (the classes are imbalanced), per-class F1, and, for systems that return probabilities, expected calibration error (Guo et al., 2017, ECE;) of the top-class probability.

4 Conflict Typing with Decision Models

A typed decision model receives a state, here the query and its numbered search results, and one or more typed questions. For a choice question it returns a probability for each option; for a yes/no question, the probability of yes. Several questions over the same state are answered in one request. We study two ways of asking for the conflict type.

Flat.

One choice question whose five options are the five categories. The instruction, the category definitions and their examples are copied word for word from the prompt of Cattan et al. (2025) (Appendix A); a test in our code fails if a single word differs. The predicted type is the most probable option, and its probability is the model’s confidence.

Tree.

The taxonomy is hierarchical, which suggests asking simpler yes/no questions in one request: differ (do the results give different answers?), compatible (could all of them be correct?), opinion (is it a contested topic with opposing views?), outdated (do they disagree because the answer changed?), and misinformation (are some results incorrect?). The five probabilities are combined in code into a distribution over the categories. Tree v1 follows the taxonomy’s order: P⁡(No conflict)=1−dP(\textit{No conflict})=1-d, P⁡(Complementary)=d​cP(\textit{Complementary})=d\,c, and the remaining mass d⁡(1−c)d(1-c) is split over the three causes in proportion to their yes-probabilities, where dd and cc are the probabilities of differ and compatible. Tree v2, chosen after inspecting Jev 1.13’s v1 answers on the development split (§6.2), asks opinion before compatible and treats misinformation as the factual conflict not explained by time: P⁡(Opinions)=d​oP(\textit{Opinions})=d\,o, P⁡(Complementary)=d⁡(1−o)​cP(\textit{Complementary})=d(1-o)c, P⁡(Outdated)=d⁡(1−o)​(1−c)​tP(\textit{Outdated})=d(1-o)(1-c)\,t and P⁡(Misinformation)=d⁡(1−o)​(1−c)​(1−t)P(\textit{Misinformation})=d(1-o)(1-c)(1-t), with oo and tt the probabilities of opinion and outdated. Both trees use the same five answers, so v2 costs nothing extra. Every decision model receives exactly the same questions and combination rules; nothing is tuned per model.

Cascade.

The decision model answers every query. The fraction ff of queries with its lowest confidence is sent to an LLM, whose answer replaces the decision model’s. The threshold is a quantile of the decision model’s confidences and uses no labels, so the whole accuracy–cost curve can be computed on the test split without leakage; we fixed f=25%f=25\% and f=50%f=50\% as the reported operating points before computing any cascade.

5 Experimental Setup

Inputs.

Every system sees the same input. As in Cattan et al. (2025), each search result is the concatenation of its URL, title, snippet, publication date (when available) and 512-token segment; results keep the dataset’s order and are numbered. For the decision models they form the state; for the LLMs they fill the paper’s prompt.

Decision models.

We run every model that the Vercel AI Gateway11 1 https://vercel.com/ai-gateway listed as a decision model on the day of the census (25 October 2026), with a pinned identifier where one exists: Jev 1.13.0 and 1.14.0 (TypeSafe AI, 2026a), Decider v1.2 and Decider Flash v1.2 (Perplexity AI, 2026b; Perplexity AI, 2026a), GPT-6 Luna Decisions (OpenAI, 2026), d1 and d1 Ultra (Liquid AI, 2026b; Liquid AI, 2026a), Decision-1 (Microsoft, 2026), Elephant-1 and Mammoth-1 (Baseten, 2026), and Classify-1 (ScaleDown, 2026). All receive the questions of §4 unchanged. Classify-1’s API accepts only a single text field, so it receives the same content as one text, the numbered results exactly as the LLMs see them. Two entries were excluded before any run. Laya, the only open decision model served by the gateway, cannot accept the task’s question, whose category definitions exceed its input limit; prior work reports it near chance without task-specific training (Duan et al., 2026; Nandakishore, 2026). typesafe-ai/jev is a floating alias of a pinned version we already run. Open-weight models that the gateway does not serve are out of scope: their cost and latency would depend on local hardware and not be comparable.

LLM baselines.

We rerun the paper’s best classifier, Gemini 2.5 Flash (Comanici et al., 2025), with the paper’s prompt verbatim, temperature 0, thinking off (the paper lists Gemini 2.5 Flash and its thinking variant separately) and, as a sensitivity check, thinking on. To compare against a current model we add Gemini 3.8 Flash, the newest Flash model available to us, at its lowest thinking level (it cannot be switched off) and at its default. The prompt asks for JSON with an explanation and a category number; answers stating the category in another format (10527 of 14,470) are parsed leniently rather than counted as errors. All models are reached through this gateway, which reports the billed cost of every request (prices may differ from the providers’ own APIs); latency is the wall-clock time of the successful request.

Protocol.

Prompts, questions, inputs and the development/test split were frozen before any test-set call, with file hashes recorded. The only setting chosen by inspecting data is tree v2, chosen on the development split and marked †\dagger in all tables. Every later addition (Gemini 3.8 Flash, the further decision models, the cascade, the diagnostics and the end-to-end test) was specified in writing before it was run, and every run is reported (Appendix B).

Statistics.

Comparisons are paired on identical queries. We report 95% bootstrap intervals over queries (Efron and Tibshirani, 1994) (10,000 resamples) and two-sided exact McNemar tests (McNemar, 1947) on per-query correctness. With 406 test queries, a 95% interval on accuracy is about ±\pm4.8 points wide, so differences under about five points are generally not significant; we report them as ties. We do not correct for multiple comparisons; with 11 models a few nominal differences at p<0.05p<0.05 are expected by chance, so we draw conclusions from patterns across models rather than from single tests.

6 Results

6.1 Decision models against the LLMs

Table 2 gives the main comparison, sorted by accuracy. Asked directly, the 11 decision models classify 50.0–67.0 % of test queries correctly (median 62.6 %). Gemini 2.5 Flash with the paper’s prompt reaches 61.3 % on the same queries. Against it, 8 decision models are statistically tied, 2 are significantly more accurate (Liquid d1 Ultra, +5.7 points, p=0.027p=0.027; Perplexity Decider v1.2, +5.4, p=0.049p=0.049), and 1, ScaleDown Classify-1, is significantly less accurate (−-11.3, p<0.001p<0.001). The decision models cost $0.04–$0.41 per thousand queries (2 were free at the time of the runs) against $1.66, and answer in 0.26–0.72  s against 1.55  s. Among the 10 models that match or exceed the paper’s LLM, those that are billed cost 4–39 ×\times less, and all are 2.6–6.0 ×\times faster.

The current Gemini 3.8 Flash is stronger: at its lowest thinking level it reaches 70.0 %, +8.6 points above Gemini 2.5 Flash (p<0.001p<0.001), at 2.2 ×\times its cost. It is significantly more accurate than 8 of the decision models; the other 3 (Liquid d1 Ultra, Perplexity Decider v1.2 and OpenAI GPT-6 Luna Decisions) trail it by 3.0 to 3.7 points without a significant difference. More thinking does not help either Gemini: Gemini 3.8 Flash at its default level scores 66.7 % (−-3.2 points against the low level, p=0.019p=0.019) and Gemini 2.5 Flash with thinking 57.9 % (p=0.19p=0.19).

Reproducing the published number.

On all 458 queries, the scope of the published result, our rerun of Gemini 2.5 Flash scores 60.7 % against the published 65.3%. The hosted model may have changed since publication, and the paper does not specify how results were joined in the prompt or whether thinking was enabled. We therefore compare every system with our rerun on identical inputs and report the published figure only as context.

Per class and calibration.

Per class (Table 3), the models differ most on Outdated information, with F1 from 27.5 to 72.7 (Gemini 3.8 Flash: 66.1). Misinformation, with 4 test instances, defeats every system: no decision model exceeds an F1 of 11.8 (Gemini 3.8 Flash: 25.0). Calibration varies more than accuracy: the expected calibration error of the flat question ranges from 0.031 to 0.188, and 7 of the 11 models are over-confident on average (mean top probability above accuracy).

6.2 Flat or tree?

Decomposing the taxonomy into yes/no questions fails for every model. Tree v1 is significantly less accurate than the flat question for 11 of the 11 models (Table 4). We had inspected the cause on the development split with one model, Jev 1.13, before any test run: it answers the compatible question yes for opinion topics almost as readily as for complementary ones (mean probability 0.69 vs. 0.81), sending 12 of 13 development opinion queries to Complementary, while the opinion question separates the two classes well (AUROC 0.83). On the test split the same model labels 89 of the 102 Conflicting opinions queries as Complementary (F1 3.8). Its misinformation question also shows the yes-bias reported for batched yes/no questions (Deußer et al., 2026): the mean probability ranged from 0.53 to 0.79 across all five classes.

Tree v2 asks opinion first and treats misinformation as the residual factual conflict. Its order was fitted on that one model’s development answers and is applied unchanged to every model. It is significantly better than the flat question for none of them, tied for 7, and significantly worse for 4. For the model it was fitted on it is tied with flat (63.5 % vs. 61.8 %, p=0.59p=0.59) and better calibrated (ECE 0.026 vs. 0.103). A repair fitted to one model’s errors helped no other model, so we use the flat question for all of them.

6.3 Confidence-gated cascades

Decision models’ confidence ranks their own errors, with AUROC from 0.64 to 0.76 (Table 5), which makes each of them a natural first stage before an LLM. Escalating the least confident quarter of queries to Gemini 3.8 Flash yields cascades statistically tied with the LLM alone for 8 of the 11 models, at 25–37 % of its cost. Escalating by confidence beats escalating the same number of queries at random for 10 of the 11 models, by up to 4.9 points; the exception is GPT-6 Luna Decisions, whose confidence barely ranks its errors (AUROC 0.65) and whose 25% cascade equals random escalation (67.0 % vs. 67.2 %). Figure 2 shows every model alone and as a cascade against the LLMs. A tie at 25% does not establish equivalence: with 406 queries, the intervals still admit losses of a few points relative to the LLM, and showing equivalence at a tight margin would need more queries than Conflicts provides.

6.4 Diagnostics

We specified three hypotheses and their tests before running them; Tables 6 and 7 give the results for every decision model’s flat question and for Gemini 3.8 Flash. An identical rerun sets the noise floor: 5 of the 11 decision models return identical answers, and the others change their predicted type on up to 9.4 % of queries with nothing changed (Gemini 3.8 Flash: 3.4 %).

Dates.

One provider documents ordering dates as a known weakness of its model (TypeSafe AI, 2026b), and we expected date handling to explain errors on Outdated. It does not. Removing every date, or adding each result’s recency rank computed in code, changes accuracy significantly in 0 of 22 tests, and recall on Outdated moves little in either direction. The models appear to recognise outdated sources from their content (phrases such as “former” or “as of”, and conflicting values), not from publication dates.

Source order.

Shuffling the results changes the predicted type on 5.4–42.1 % of queries (pooled over two seeds), above the noise floor for all 11 models; Gemini 3.8 Flash flips on 9.4 %. Paired on the same shuffles, 4 decision models flip significantly more often than the LLM, 1 less often, and 6 no differently. The flips rarely change accuracy: 2 of 22 shuffle tests are significant, both for GPT-6 Luna Decisions (−-4.7 and −-5.7 points). Order sensitivity is therefore a property of individual models rather than of the class, and a deployment should test it.

Planted false sources.

Conflicts has too few Misinformation queries to evaluate. We construct them: in 96 No conflict test queries whose gold answer appears in some result, we rewrite one such result so that it states a plausible wrong answer, produced by a third model (GPT-4.1-mini) so that no classifier judges its own text. The expected label becomes Misinformation. As hard labels, the decision models call 7.3–66.7 % of planted copies misinformation (Gemini 3.8 Flash: 52.1 %). Net of false alarms on the clean copies, their detection (Youden index) ranges from +0.052 to +0.490 against +0.490 for the LLM; paired on the same queries, 8 are significantly worse and 3 are statistically tied. The probabilities tell a different story: the probability of Misinformation separates planted from clean copies with AUROC 0.66–0.86, at least 0.75 for 10 of the 11. The models notice the planted source but rarely make Misinformation their top answer, so a lower threshold on that probability, chosen on development data, would recover detections.

Version stability.

One provider serves two pinned versions. Jev 1.14 differs from 1.13 by −-2.2 points with the flat question (p=0.12p=0.12) and −-0.7 with tree v2 (p=0.66p=0.66), with the same failure of tree v1 (Table 4): the conclusions do not depend on which version is served.

6.5 End to end: do cheaper types keep the gain?

With Gemini 2.5 Flash as the generator, Cattan et al. (2025) report that the share of answers following the expected behaviour rises from 65.7% without a type (Vanilla) to 75.1% with types predicted by Gemini 2.5 Flash (Pipeline) and 88.0% with gold types (Oracle). Can a decision model be the Pipeline’s predictor without losing this gain?

Setup.

The generator is Gemini 2.5 Flash (thinking off, temperature 0) on the same numbered results. Vanilla uses their answer prompt verbatim; a type adds its definition and expected behaviour from their paper (Appendix A). We generate one answer per test query for Vanilla and for each type (2,436 answers); a predictor receives the answer for the type it predicts, so predictors differ only through their predictions. As in their study, an LLM judge (Zheng et al., 2023) (Gemini 2.5 Flash) decides whether the answer follows the gold type’s expected behaviour, given the query, the type’s description, an adherent and a non-adherent example, but not the sources; a second prompt checks whether it contains the gold answer (202 queries). On 100 answers labelled blind by two annotators, who agree on 92 % (Cohen’s κ=0.67\kappa=0.67; Cohen, 1960), the judge agrees with their majority on 92 % (Cattan et al.: 89%; κ=0.46\kappa=0.46, as 90 % of answers follow; Appendix B). Our protocol also specified a second judge, Gemini 3.8 Flash (thinking low), which agrees less often (87 %); we report both.

Results.

With the primary judge the ordering of Cattan et al. (2025) reappears (Table 8): Vanilla 87.9 %, Pipeline 91.6 % (+3.7 points, p=0.032p=0.032), Oracle 95.3 % (+7.4, p<0.001p<0.001); our judge rates answers higher than theirs, which compresses the differences. Replacing Gemini 2.5 Flash as the predictor changes little: 10 of the 11 decision models are tied with it (−-3.9 to +0.7 points), and only the least accurate classifier, ScaleDown Classify-1, is significantly worse (−-3.9, p=0.011p=0.011). With a quarter of queries escalated to Gemini 3.8 Flash, 11 of the 11 cascades are tied with it (−-1.0 to +0.7). Gains concentrate on Conflicting opinions (Vanilla 82.4 %, Oracle 97.1 %) and Outdated (72.7 % to 87.3 %); no condition lowers answer recall (90.6–93.1 %). With the second judge, gold types still help (+5.7, p<0.001p<0.001) but predicted types do not (Pipeline 89.7 %, Vanilla 91.1 %, p=0.47p=0.47), and 11 of the 11 decision models remain tied with the Gemini 2.5 Flash Pipeline. The size of the gain from predicted types thus depends on the judge; that a decision model can replace the LLM as the predictor does not.

7 Discussion

What decision models offer as conflict classifiers.

Conflict typing sits on the critical path of every search-augmented answer, so its latency and cost add to every request. Most hosted decision models classify a query with about ten retrieved pages in under half a second, for at most $0.41 per thousand queries, with the accuracy of the LLM used in the original study. When the accuracy of a current LLM is required, a decision model’s confidence is usually good enough to route only its uncertain queries to the LLM, which recovers most of the gap at a quarter to a third of the LLM’s cost. End to end, the cheaper types cost no measurable answer quality (§6.5).

Choosing among decision models.

The class is not uniform. Accuracy spans 50.0–67.0 %, and the model at the bottom is significantly worse than the paper’s LLM. Two properties that matter in deployment vary independently of accuracy: calibration (ECE 0.031–0.188) and how well confidence ranks errors, which decides whether a cascade helps at all. One of the most accurate models has confidence that is no better than random for escalation. A model for this task should therefore be chosen on all three, measured on the deployment’s own data, not on accuracy alone.

How to ask.

The direct choice question was the reliable format for every model. The yes/no decomposition looked natural but failed for all of them; the repaired tree encodes choices fitted to one model on a small development split and did not help any other. For a new decision model we would start from the flat question.

What the diagnostics change.

Dates turned out not to matter: outdated sources are recognised from their content. Sensitivity to source order is real but differs so much between models that it has to be measured for each one. A single false source is the subtle case, visible in the probabilities but rarely in the top label. With 4 natural Misinformation test queries, that type is the one a deployment would most need to calibrate on its own data.

Limitations.

(i) Conflicts is small: with 406 test queries, differences under about five points are not significant, and the cascades can be shown close to, but not formally equivalent to, the LLM. (ii) The label distribution reflects how the queries were selected, not real search traffic, and the dataset has only five natural Misinformation queries; our planted variant tests one kind of misinformation (an entity or value substituted in a single source). (iii) The census covers the decision models one gateway served on one day. Hosted models change without notice: several identifiers are unversioned, two models were free during our runs, and our rerun of Gemini 2.5 Flash scores below the published figure. Providers do not disclose model sizes or training data, so we cannot explain the differences between models. (iv) The end-to-end test uses one generator and LLM judges, validated on 100 answers, that do not see the search results; as in the original study, the primary judge is the generator’s own model, which may favour its answers (Panickssery et al., 2024). The size of the gain from predicted types depends on the judge, and we do not measure factual grounding, the third metric of Cattan et al. (2025). (v) Not every system is deterministic: identical requests changed up to 9.4 % of a decision model’s predictions, and 3.4 % of Gemini 3.8 Flash’s.

8 Conclusion

We tested every typed decision model hosted on one gateway as a classifier of knowledge-conflict types, using the benchmark authors’ protocol and the same inputs as the LLMs. Most match the LLM of the original study. They do so at a small fraction of its cost and latency. They trail the current LLM, but for most of them a confidence-gated cascade recovers that gap at a quarter to a third of the LLM’s cost, and given to a generator, their types yield answers that follow the expected behaviour as often as the LLM’s. Future work should measure the gain from predicted types with judges that see the sources, and test whether a decision model’s probabilities can steer a generator between expected behaviours when the type is uncertain.

Ethics and Broader Impact

The planted-misinformation variant rewrites one retrieved page per query to state a wrong answer. It uses public data and factual substitutions on non-sensitive questions, and is released with clear labels. All queries in Conflicts are safe by construction (Cattan et al., 2025). Cheap conflict classification could be misused to suppress minority viewpoints; the expected behaviour for Conflicting opinions is to present all of them.

Appendix A Prompts and Questions

LLM prompt.

The conflict-type prompt of Cattan et al. (2025), copied from the paper’s source with only the LaTeX bold markers removed. The asterisks are the prompt’s own Markdown emphasis and were sent as written. {search_results} is filled with the numbered results.

Decision models, flat.

One choice question. Its instruction is the first paragraph of the prompt above; its options are the five category definitions with their examples, word for word.

Decision models, tree.

Five yes/no questions asked in one request over the same state.

Planted wrong answers.

Prompt sent to GPT-4.1-mini (temperature 0) to obtain a plausible wrong answer for each No conflict query whose gold answer appears in a result. The answer is then replaced, as whole words and case-insensitively, in the title, snippet and text of one such result chosen with a fixed seed. Queries whose gold answer is yes or no are excluded.

End to end: generation.

Vanilla is the answer prompt of Cattan et al. (2025) (their Figure 3) verbatim. For a type, the line below is inserted before the query; the description is the type’s definition and expected behaviour from their §2, with citations and worked examples removed.

End to end: judges.

The behaviour judge, shown for Misinformation; for the other types the description and the two examples change. The examples are those of Cattan et al. (2025), Table 3, except for No conflict, which has none there and for which we wrote one pair. The answer-recall judge follows.

Appendix B Protocol Record

The development/test split, the prompt and question texts and the combination rules were frozen with recorded file hashes before any test-set call. Changes after that point were limited to the following, each logged with its reason before results were computed: (1) Gemini 2.5 Flash with thinking added as a sensitivity check; (2) the answer parser made lenient for category statements outside the requested JSON, applied to stored answers without new calls (no strictly formatted answer changed); (3) Gemini 3.8 Flash added at two thinking levels; (4) the cascade, its operating points and its controls; (5) the diagnostics, with one amendment before any planted run: whole-word matching and the exclusion of yes/no answers, after substring matching was found to alter unrelated numbers; (6) a second Jev version and four further decision models, run with the frozen questions; (7) the remaining five decision models listed by the gateway, completing the census, with the diagnostics extended to every decision model’s flat question, and one amendment before any run: Classify-1 receives the same content as a single text field, which its API requires; (8) the end-to-end test, specified before any generation call: generator, prompts, judges, the 100-answer validation sample and its threshold, and a second judge (Gemini 3.8 Flash) to be reported with the first. Prompts were checked on the development split for errors only; none was changed after scoring. All runs are reported.

Judge validation.

The 100 answers were drawn with a fixed seed, 20 per gold type and about half from Vanilla, and shown to the annotators with the query, the gold type’s description and expected behaviour, and the answer, without the judge’s verdict or the condition. Annotator 2’s sheet showed another item’s answer for one item; that label is excluded. The primary judge agrees with the annotators’ majority (a tie counting as follows, as fixed before labelling) on 92 %, with annotator 1 on 91 % and with annotator 2 on 87 %; the second judge on 87 %, 84 % and 82 %. Code, splits, prompts, cached responses and per-query outputs are released.
